To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The mental syllabary is a concept which has to be refined, as it does not seem to be a storage of syllable sized motor plans, but rather a storage of syllabic units that can be assembled into syllables; 2) The syllable is not the smallest motor unit in speech production, but rather the syllable onset; 3) The mental syllable is not a storage of ready-made motor plans, but a storage of units that can be combined in
syllable structure, not syllable frequency, is a crucial factor for the motor control of speech.
the syllable is an important constituent of speech motor control processes in reading aloud.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the brain's "mental syllabaries" in overt reading of pseudohomographs, i.e., pseudowords.
the role of the phonological syllable in speech production and speech perception.
the role of the brain in the control of speech production.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the syllable is a relevant unit of speech production, but that its relevance is not absolute and that its role is not necessarily restricted to high-frequency syllables.
the syllable is a functional unit of speech motor control and that it is stored as a ready-made motor plan, but that it is not the smallest unit in speech production.
syllables are important units in the control of speech production, but their influence on the neural control of speech production may be modulated by the frequency and the complexity of the syllable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
syllable structure, but not frequency, is an important factor in speech motor control processes.
syllable frequency is not a major determinant of syllable motor planning, but that the motor system seems to prefer syllables with simple onsets.
the brain uses syllable-sized motor plans, which are stored in the mental syllabary.
The main takeaway from our work is that
syllable frequency and syllable structure are not independent factors in speech motor control, but interact.
syllables with a simple onset (CV, CVC) are more easily accessible from the mental syllabary than those with a complex onset.
the syllable, as the most basic unit of speech production, is an important component in speech motor control processes.
